note: Wallachia became an Ottoman tributary in stages following the Battle of Nicopolis (1396), though Mircea the Elder had already acknowledged Ottoman suzerainty earlier (1393). The arrangement — paying haraç (tribute) and providing military contingents while maintaining internal self-governance — was periodically disrupted by resistance. Vlad III 'the Impaler' (Dracula) famously broke from Ottoman suzerainty and impaled Ottoman envoys (1459), triggering a massive Ottoman invasion. Wallachia's mountain passes and forest terrain, combined with diplomatic maneuver between the Ottomans and Hungary, allowed it to maintain autonomy through the tribute system.

_quarry.structural_significance: Wallachia's tributary status models the 'autonomous principality' approach that allows Romanian culture and Orthodox Christianity to survive the Ottoman period; Vlad III's resistance becomes the core of the Dracula legend that shapes Western perception of Transylvania; the principality's survival through tribute diplomacy creates the Romanian national continuity
